title: GPU stalls, intermittent OOMs, and KV-cache coherence triage - Arclight Systems
summary: Deep technical triage of intermittent soft OOMs and GPU stalls observed on Arclight's Redwood Private deployment. Discussed KV-cache desync, batching heuristics, prefetch/backpressure, and retry semantics. Agreed on reproducibility harness, additional logs, and a short pilot patch for kernel fallback and conservative batch sizing.
topics: batch size heuristics and autoscale interplay

transcript:
HEADER:
Date: 2026-10-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Meeting title: GPU stalls, intermittent OOMs, and KV-cache coherence triage - Arclight Systems
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Ortega (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (Redwood PM), Maya Chen (Arclight SRE), David Hsu (Arclight ML Infra), Priya Nair (Arclight Security), Evan Park (Arclight Backend)

AUTO SUMMARY (auto): Brief triage of repeated soft OOMs / cuda launch timeouts on Arclight private cluster. Focus areas: KV cache race during prefetch, batching spikes causing fragmentation, watchdog timeouts vs hard OOMs, retry semantics for long-context chat, and on-prem networking impacts.

[00:00] Samir: all right thanks everyone for joining, let's do a quick roll call — Lina and I from Redwood, Jordan's on for platform stuff. Maya, David, Priya, Evan from Arclight?
[00:10] Maya: yep that's us, thanks for fitting this in. we've been seeing a bunch of those intermittent failures mid-load, usually during lunchtime spikes, so hoping we can get to root cause.
[00:20] Lina: cool, can you describe the most recent failure pattern, maybe give a concrete request id or time window?
[00:30] Maya: sure — on Oct 19th at 12:06 UTC we had 17 failures in 2 minutes across three nodes, errors labelled as 'CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT' and a handful flagged as "soft OOM" by the runtime. some calls recovered on retry.
[00:52] David: adding detail — the requests were long-context chat, seq len around 18k tokens, with batch sizes varying from 1 up to 12 as clients burst. importantly we saw KV cache eviction churn around the same time, maybe due to memory fragmentation.
[01:10] Lina: interesting. we suspect interplay between large kv cache allocations and variable batching. if prefetch hits an eviction path while another request holds pointers it can create transient invalidation — usually that's handled by our kvcache locks but in some older kernels there's a race.
[01:35] Priya: from security side we also want to confirm no user PII leaked into logs; keep any dumps redacted. also SOC2 and key management questions — we need KMS call traces for the time window.
[01:50] Samir: absolutely — we'll sanitize. quick question: are you running Redwood Private with the on-prem package or VPC-connected control plane?
[01:58] Maya: on-prem, fully air-gapped except for KMS via a peered route. we also have strict egress rules, and our infra team recently changed MTU on the internal fabric.
[02:12] Jordan: MTU changes could explain NCCL timeouts if large collectives are on the path. even if the model is single-GPU, some orchestration paths still use NCCL for device discovery and health checks, which can trigger weird hangs.
[02:28] Evan: we did bump MTU to 9000 recently. not sure if any blackhole happened but we'll check.
[02:35] Lina: ok let's walk through our hypothesis list: (1) batching spikes + large seqs = memory fragmentation -> soft OOMs; (2) kvcache eviction race during prefetch leading to stale pointers -> kernel faults/timeouts; (3) NCCL/network MTU causing watchdog to misclassify as launch timeout; (4) driver version mismatch causing library hang.
[03:05] David: our driver is 535.86 and CUDA 12.2, kernels are Ubuntu 22.04. we've seen a few driver upgrade notes from NV about 535.x that mention launch time parameter regressions.
[03:20] Lina: ok good to know. one immediate mitigation is conservative batch capping and forced KV prewarm to reduce eviction churn. we can also push a runtime patch that adds a safe path: when kernel launch fails we fall back to a slower but more robust SLOW_KERNEL that uses less workspace and avoids the failing code path.
[03:45] Maya: would that fallback be transparent to the client? any perf hit?
[03:50] Lina: largely transparent — latency increases for affected requests (20-40% in our tests) but it avoids node resets and hard OOMs. it's a defensive patch for a canary rollout.
[04:05] Samir: also want to call out retry semantics — are your clients auto-retrying at the HTTP layer? we prefer idempotent retry at the Redwood SDK layer with a unique request id so we can dedupe at serving if needed.
[04:20] Evan: they do three retries with exponential backoff in the gateway, but no deterministic id for the model call itself.
[04:30] David: that means retries can increase peak concurrency and worsen fragmentation, so we should treat that as a contributor.
[04:40] Lina: exactly. for long-context workloads, retries are dangerous unless deduped. we recommend renewing the request id in the header and enabling SDK-level dedupe or a short sticky token.
[04:55] [05:00] Maya: can you explain what you mean by 'KV prewarm'? we've tried warm caches but maybe we're missing the right pattern.
[05:10] Lina: prewarm means issuing small synthetic requests that allocate the KV cache for the model and typical sequence lengths before traffic spikes. also set a conservative eviction watermark so small bursts don't evict large prefixes.
[05:28] Samir: we'll share a script for KV prewarm and an instrumentation guide.
[05:35] David: on the logs — we saw many 'device reset' messages from the watchdog around the timestamp. are those generated after the kernel launch timeout?
[05:45] Lina: usually, yes. watchdog sees a long-running stream and triggers driver-side termination. but the root cause may be a kernel spin or waiting on an invalid pointer. stack traces are critical here.
[05:58] Priya: about logs, what level do we need? we can't keep verbose debug on in prod for too long.
[06:05] Jordan: just for a short window — kernel-fallback logs, kvcache lifecycle (alloc/free events), CUDA stack traces, and any NCCL/all-reduce timeouts. we'll provide log redaction guidance so you can scrub PII.
[06:20] Maya: noted. Evan will attach dmesg and system journal for that window.
[06:25] Evan: yes i'll collect and put into the ticket.
[06:30] [06:45] Lina: quick note on quantization: are you serving quantized variants for cost reasons? quantized kernels sometimes change workspace layouts and can reveal alignment bugs, especially with int8 fused ops.
[06:55] David: we do mixed-int8 on a subset of models. the failures seem to hit both FP16 and int8 paths, so maybe not purely quantization.
[07:10] Samir: ok that's useful. next up, let's split into immediate mitigations and longer investigations. immediate: reduce max-batch to 6 for long-context routes, enable KV prewarm, and turn on conservative eviction watermark. medium: runtime patch with kernel fallback, instrumentation. long: repro harness and driver matrix testing.
[07:35] Maya: can you explain the fallback patch mechanics at a high-level?
[07:40] Lina: sure — when a kernel fails to launch or returns a known failure code, runtime will log, increment a per-node soft-failure counter, and route subsequent similar shapes to the fallback kernel for N minutes. If soft-failure persists above threshold we mark the node as degraded and shift traffic. The fallback kernel uses a different memory allocation pattern and avoids the code path that triggers the hang.
[08:10] David: does that interact with autoscaler? we don't want cascade where degraded nodes get evicted and autoscale thrashes.
[08:20] Jordan: good point — we'll adjust autoscaler thresholds during the canary: prefer adding capacity over evicting, and temporarily disable aggressive scale-in for the test.
[08:35] [09:00] Maya: curious about one line in your docs about prefix/KV caching and continuous batching — is it possible that continuous batching pulls stale KV pages into an already-inflight allocation?
[09:10] Lina: yes if the batching layer aggregates requests with different sequence-length distributions and the kvcache eviction is concurrent, you can see pointer reuse that the allocator isn't expecting. our newer allocators check for staleness but older kernels may not.
[09:30] Evan: we can try forcing single-shape batching for the most frequent long-context route in staging.
[09:35] Samir: great. moving on, can we also capture driver and runtime versions and correlate?
[09:40] David: driver 535.86, CUDA 12.2, runtime 1.14.0 (Redwood), kernel 5.15.
[09:52] Lina: runtime 1.14.0 has a kvcache patch we shipped in 1.14.2; surprising you're still on 1.14.0. the patch adds per-request KV guards. we can backport a targeted fix into a 1.14.0-compatible patch if needed.
[10:10] Maya: we'd prefer a minimal patch and can handle a canary machine set.
[10:18] Jordan: we'll prepare a patch that only enables verbose logging + a single guard check and a disabled fallback by default. then if logs show the race we can flip fallback on for the canary.
[10:30] [11:00] David: how much perf regression with guard checks?
[11:05] Lina: negligible for the common case, maybe 2-5% tail. fallback kernel is the one with bigger impact.
[11:12] Priya: security question — any additional attack surface with the kvcache debug mode?
[11:18] Samir: no persistent external surface; debug mode collects ephemeral traces and we recommend enabling it only in staging/canary with redacted dumps. no keys are included.
[11:30] Evan: regarding NCCL, should we run a simple all-reduce synthetic to validate MTU and path?
[11:36] Jordan: yes please; we'll include an NCCL char test in the repro harness. also run with tcp and ibverbs if applicable.
[11:45] Maya: timeline — how soon can you provide the patched binary?
[11:50] Lina: we can get a first-instrumented binary within 6 business days, so target Nov 2nd. after you run the canary we'll iterate.
[12:00] Samir: ok let's recap and call out owners. Lina will own the binary/patch and logging instructions, Jordan will own the repro harness, Maya/Evan will produce logs and enable the canary machines, David will coordinate driver info and batch config.
[12:15] Maya: noted, we'll also scrub logs for PII before sharing.
[12:20] Priya: we'll need an encrypted s3 or secure upload path for debug artifacts; can you provide an endpoint that meets our compliance requirements?
[12:30] Samir: yes, we'll send a presigned URL with limited TTL and a checklist for redaction.
[12:40] David: one last quick note — our gateway retries are a simple 3x. we'll switch to 1 retry and add request-id in the header during the test window to reduce compounded load.
[12:50] Lina: thanks, that will help a lot.
[12:55] Samir: ok pulling together next steps and we'll follow up with the patch link and repro instructions. thanks everyone.

AUTO ACTIONS: shared items and owners captured in action_items.
